# The Tale of the River Keeper and the Mountain Smith

Long ago, when the world was young, a River Keeper controlled all flowing water, while a Mountain Smith held dominion over precious metals. The Smith desperately needed water to cool her forge and craft tools for the villages below. The River Keeper needed metal tools to maintain the river channels that prevented devastating floods.

One season, the River Keeper approached the Smith with a proposal: "Send me your finest tools, and I shall send water flowing to your forge threefold." The Smith hesitated. If she sent her tools and received nothing, her forge would die. But if she withheld, both would suffer.

The Smith chose trust. She sent her three best tools downstream. True to his word, the River Keeper opened channels that brought abundant water to the mountain. In gratitude, the Smith forged new tools and sent half back to the River Keeper.

This exchange continued for generations. Each season they gave freely, and each season both prospered. The villages below flourished with well-made tools and protected waterways.

The elders say: *Trust flows like water—when given freely, it returns threefold. When hoarded, both the giver and receiver run dry.*

The rivers agreed to share their powers. Clear Waters would send portions of its essence to Deep Currents, trusting it would return enriched water to nourish the valleys below. Encouraged, Clear Waters sent more in the second season. Deep Currents again returned generously, and prosperity spread across the land.

But in the third season, Deep Currents grew proud. "Why should I return what my power has multiplied?" it wondered. When Clear Waters sent its largest offering yet, Deep Currents kept nearly everything, returning only a trickle.

Clear Waters, betrayed, withdrew its trust and sent nothing more. Deep Currents, without new water to multiply, began to stagnate. Both rivers diminished, and the valleys withered.

The mountain spring whispered: "Trust is the source from which all abundance flows. Break it, and even magic runs dry."
